items.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool for SQLite
items.summary: sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of a SQLite database over SSH without creating a local full copy, using a protocol similar to rsync.
items.why: It enables efficient remote backups and synchronization on disk‑constrained systems.
items.desc: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. items.title: NYT warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
items.summary: NYT photographers refuse to use Photoshop AI features, insisting on presenting photos as taken.
items.why: It shows a media policy limiting AI-based photo editing.
items.desc: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.) items.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
items.summary: Partial fine-tuning of a small subset of layers in an AWGN-trained autoencoder removes the error floor when adapting to Rayleigh fading channels.
items.why: It reduces the time and energy needed to adapt AI-native communication systems to new channel conditions.
items.desc: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. items.title: Tokenisation Is Not in APX
items.summary: The authors prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate optimal tokenisation within any constant factor, making tokenisation APX‑hard.
items.why: It reveals fundamental limits on efficiently finding near‑optimal tokenisers, influencing future algorithm design.
items.desc: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: Can Image Generation Help Visual Reasoning? An Empirical Study
items.summary: Adding generated helper images reduces mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points across 13 vision‑language model and generator pairs, with declines on nine of ten tasks.
items.why: It reveals that naïvely augmenting visual reasoning with generated images can degrade performance, guiding future multimodal model development.
items.desc: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

items.title: Attack Policy Selection Can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
items.summary: The study shows that the false negative rate of an OpenAI monitor ranges from 0.5% to 23% depending on the attack policy generation method and optimization level, indicating that monitor evaluation can be misleading.
items.why: It shows that limited attack methods can give false confidence in AI safety monitors.
items.desc: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. items.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
items.summary: The DART method recovers 37% more hard math problems than Monte Carlo sampling while reducing the cost per accepted trace by 30%.
items.why: It expands coverage of difficult problems and supplies high‑quality data for post‑training LLMs.
items.desc: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer Introduces New Loop Attention Mechanism
items.summary: The Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT) uses key‑value memory across loops to improve the expressivity‑efficiency trade‑off, and its U‑shaped variant outperforms OLMo3 in 400 B‑token pretraining.
items.why: It offers a scalable way to enhance transformer performance while reducing computational overhead, important for building larger LLMs.
items.desc: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. items.title: μ-Bench Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Voice Agents
items.summary: Proprietary voice agents reach about 62‑65% joint task success on the μ‑Bench benchmark, while open‑weight models fall below 20%.
items.why: It shows the performance gap of open‑source voice agents in multi‑user scenarios and provides a standard benchmark for future improvements.
items.desc: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. items.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness Using Latent Space Representations
items.summary: Compressed latent‑space embeddings of Sentinel‑1 SAR imagery detect vessels with ROC‑AUC 0.95, localise them within ~300 m for ships longer than 100 m, and classify AIS type codes with 62% accuracy.
items.why: It shows that geospatial foundation models can process satellite data efficiently, reducing data‑gravity bottlenecks and enabling faster maritime monitoring.
items.desc: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. items.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
items.summary: The authors propose a hybrid decision‑tree architecture that mixes feature‑based and case‑based splits and introduce a selective case‑based split method, which outperforms standard decision trees on diverse tabular datasets.
items.why: It provides a more accurate yet still interpretable alternative for tabular machine‑learning tasks.
items.desc: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge‑Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.summary: The paper introduces DRBench Pro, a benchmark that evaluates deep research agents on structured knowledge coverage across 144 cases, with the best agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage.
items.why: It offers a standardized way to measure and improve how AI agents gather and synthesize knowledge, guiding future agent development.
items.desc: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. items.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
items.summary: The authors present OmniAct, a manipulation policy that conditions on a robot’s kinematic graph to enable a single policy to control up to one million diverse robot embodiments.
items.why: It demonstrates a scalable approach for transferring control policies across vastly different robot morphologies, advancing generalist robot learning.
items.desc: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. items.title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
items.summary: DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM that jointly generates transcripts, timestamps and speaker visual descriptions, achieves diarization comparable to Gemini 4 Argon and significantly higher timestamp accuracy.
items.why: It improves automated video captioning and speaker identification, enabling more accurate subtitles and multimodal AI applications.
items.desc: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

items.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
items.summary: The paper demonstrates that long‑horizon policies can be distilled from a teacher's actions alone, allowing a student model to later reason with its own chain‑of‑thought while matching the teacher’s behavior and improving task success rates.
items.why: It shows a cheaper way to transfer reasoning abilities from closed models, boosting the performance of smaller agents.
items.desc: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. items.title: BriConstrain: Geometrically Constrained Decoding for Autoregressive Brick Assembly Generation
items.summary: BriConstrain introduces a decoding method that dynamically restricts a pretrained language model’s token probabilities to ensure geometrically valid LEGO brick placements during generation.
items.why: It lets language models create physically plausible LEGO designs without costly resampling, advancing controllable generative modeling.
items.desc: Language models can generate LEGO$^\circledR$ assemblies from text, but their builds often contain parts that collide or attach to nothing. The usual approach of rejecting and resampling invalid placements discards decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. We present BriConstrain, a constrained decoding method that restricts a pretrained language model's next-token probabilities before sampling, steering it towards valid placements. Because the validity of a brick placement depends on the non-predetermined build state, it cannot be compiled into a fixed grammar and must be checked dynamically. However, checking the validity of a brick before sampling is challenging as the space of valid placements is combinatorially large and cannot be enumerated exhaustively. Our key idea is to narrow the search space by constraining how parts attach rather than which parts attach to each other. Concretely, given the model's predictions of the currently placed part, and the previously placed parent it wants to connect to, we constrain the model's choice of how they attach. items.title: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Boost MATH-500 Accuracy, Complementing Large Model Weight Edit
items.summary: Fine‑tuning only the highest‑gradient ~140 k weights of Qwen3.5‑0.8B with 50 MATH examples raises its thinking‑mode MATH‑500 accuracy to 39‑45% in minutes, and combined with a large weight edit reaches over 52%.
items.why: It demonstrates that very small, targeted updates can dramatically improve reasoning performance in tiny LLMs, offering a low‑cost path to stronger models.
items.desc: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. items.title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report
items.summary: The paper introduces SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that stores full dialogue messages in non‑overlapping chunks and retrieves complementary evidence via query‑time lexical expansion with BM25 (and an optional embedding‑based scoring variant), without any model‑based memory construction.
items.why: It allows efficient, lossless retrieval of scattered conversational facts while avoiding costly inference steps.
items.desc: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. items.title: MetaFORGE: Meta-Learning Framework Optimizes Automated MPI Code Generation
items.summary: MetaFORGE iteratively refines natural‑language specifications with execution‑grounded rewards, improving static‑analysis quality, runtime performance, and load balance over zero‑shot and TextGrad baselines across six MPI tasks.
items.why: It boosts the correctness and efficiency of LLM‑generated parallel code, reducing developer effort and runtime costs.
items.desc: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. items.title: Draft Calibration Improves Speculative Decoding Speed for LLM Serving
items.summary: Applying temperature scaling to draft models reduces the distribution gap with the target model, increasing token acceptance rates and accelerating speculative decoding.
items.why: Higher acceptance rates make LLM inference faster and more cost‑effective for developers and services.
items.desc: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. items.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
items.summary: Adding learned temporal conditioning tokens to a chess transformer improves move prediction accuracy under time pressure and better predicts thinking time and resignations.
items.why: It shows that incorporating clock information makes AI models more realistic at mimicking human play, especially under time constraints.
items.desc: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. items.title: Delegent: A Multi‑Agent Harness That Reduces Cost Without Sacrificing Performance
items.summary: Delegent lets a frontier model delegate easy subtasks to a small language model, cutting frontier compute cost by up to 67% for coding and 59% for search with no loss in performance.
items.why: It offers a simple, model‑agnostic way to lower inference expenses for complex AI agents, making large‑scale deployments more affordable.
items.desc: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. items.title: EventDiffusion Learns Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
items.summary: EventDiffusion directly learns to generate realistic asynchronous event streams from video recordings using a three‑stage diffusion process.
items.why: It enables more diverse and faithful synthetic event‑camera data, accelerating research and development in high‑speed vision.
items.desc: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. items.summary: Language models do not detect their own errors when verbalizing confidence, and uncertainty tokens do not reliably steer them to correct mistakes.
items.why: It shows that confidence signals are unreliable for self‑monitoring and steering in LLMs.
items.desc: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the o

items.title: CTLink: A Text‑Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
items.summary: CTLink, a text‑prompted 3D segmentation model, outperformed prior models and achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) in the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge.
items.why: It enables automatic visual localization of report findings, streamlining radiology interpretation and research.
items.desc: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. items.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
items.summary: The new ActSpace‑Bench benchmark shows that top vision‑language models can actively explore to gather evidence for spatial questions, but their performance remains far below that of optimal oracle routes.
items.why: It provides the first systematic measure of VLMs' ability to purposefully seek information, a key step toward more autonomous and reliable AI agents.
items.desc: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. items.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
items.summary: ToolSmith automatically generates new multimodal search tools, boosting benchmark performance over a minimal base library.
items.why: It cuts down manual tool engineering and lets agents adapt to new query types and evidence formats.
items.desc: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

items.title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
items.summary: The paper introduces Neurovascular Codes, a shared EEG representation that enables stochastic generation of fMRI signals and improves Pearson correlation with real fMRI by up to 19% over strong baselines.
items.why: It provides a more accurate way to translate EEG data into fMRI, advancing multimodal brain imaging and potential clinical diagnostics.
items.desc: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. items.title: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
items.summary: A two‑stage LLM system with conformal calibration achieves 0.899 AUARC on Spider, enabling reliable confidence estimates and controlled abstention for Text‑to‑SQL queries.
items.why: It provides a practical method to detect and avoid incorrect database queries generated by AI, improving the safety and reliability of AI‑driven data access.
items.desc: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899

items.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
items.summary: CO-GRAFT reveals that query generation accounts for less than 15% of the total reinforcement‑learning performance gain in LLM search agents.
items.why: Understanding which components drive RL improvements helps researchers focus future work on the most impactful parts of search agents.
items.desc: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. items.title: TipSweep Enables Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Transformer Block Counts
items.summary: The authors propose TipSweep, a method that predicts optimal learning rates for any number of trainable transformer blocks using scaling rules (k⁻¹ for FP32 master weights, k⁻¹/² for BF16), allowing LR tuning by training only the last block.
items.why: It dramatically cuts the compute and memory cost of learning‑rate search during LLM post‑training fine‑tuning.
items.desc: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. items.title: Laya Model’s Name Shortcut Is Driven by Mid‑Layer Attention to Marker Tokens
items.summary: Blocking attention from marker tokens to their own name tokens in layers 14‑17 reduces Laya’s name‑shortcut reliance from 67% to 16% while keeping overall accuracy at 90%.
items.why: Demonstrates that targeted attention interventions can curb spurious shortcuts without harming performance, aiding model interpretability and robustness.
items.desc: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. items.title: Serialization and the Character-System: Measuring Narrative Concentration in French Fiction (1800–1940)
items.summary: Analysis of 12,011 French novels from 1800 to 1940 reveals a U‑shaped trend in narrative concentration, with a dip in the 1850s‑60s and a rise toward the turn of the century.
items.why: It shows how AI‑driven network and NLP methods can quantify literary trends at scale.
items.desc: Every novel divides a finite quantity of narrative attention among its characters, and whether the shape of that division, between a narrative organized around a single figure and one spread across a crowd, has a history is far less settled than the abundance of critical commentary on protagonists might suggest. We operationalize Woloch's notion of the character-system, the distribution of narrative attention across a novel's cast structured by the tension between "the one" and "the many", as the inequality (Gini coefficient) of the PageRank distribution over a character network. We trace this measure of structural concentration across 12,011 French novels published between 1800 and 1940, drawn from the Hors d'usage corpus of Gallica fiction. Over the long nineteenth century the trajectory is U-shaped, with concentration declining to a trough in the 1850s-1860s and rising again through the turn of the century. The change is small, comparable to the difference between a novel built on two co-equal protagonists and one built on a single protagonist, but it is robust to the character cutoff, corpus density, cast size, and author effects. items.summary: The study finds that miscalibrated attention temperature, not architectural changes, explains apparent performance gains in zero-shot context extension, and calibrating temperature removes those advantages.
items.why: It shows that evaluation of context‑extension methods must control for temperature calibration to avoid misleading conclusions.
items.desc: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. items.desc: Release v5.24.0 New Model additions Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint ( TML-d24-varloop-research ) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. Links: Documentation | Blog Post | HF Blog Post Add Inkling2 Mini ( #51050 ) by @guarin Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. items.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without Finite Variance
items.summary: The authors propose a black‑box reduction that turns any finite‑variance linear regression algorithm into one that achieves optimal rates under heavy‑tailed noise with only a finite α‑moment, matching a minimax lower bound and remaining computationally efficient.
items.why: It enables reliable regression on heavy‑tailed data without knowing noise moments, expanding robust ML toolkits.
items.desc: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ \lesssim_α ν^{1/α} \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. items.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
items.summary: MemOnce introduces a memory encoder‑decoder with sparse attention that stores only a small subset of final‑layer hidden states and decodes them into KV caches, achieving linear‑time inference and drastically reduced GPU memory usage for LLMs.
items.why: It enables more efficient long‑horizon and continual LLM deployments by cutting memory and compute costs.
items.desc: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. items.title: Non-Penetrating World Models
items.summary: A lightweight add‑on (NoPeWorld) that reads frozen diffusion‑transformer states to block penetrating actions reduces physical violations in video world models from 74% to 16% and generalizes zero‑shot.
items.why: It provides a simple, effective way to improve safety and reliability of interactive video world models used in AI agents.
items.desc: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. items.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
items.summary: Model Carving jointly learns transformer weights and architecture via scalar gates, yielding smaller heterogeneous models that achieve lower validation loss than dense models using up to 1.7× more compute and outperform pruning or distillation baselines.
items.why: It provides a way to automatically discover more efficient transformer structures during training, reducing compute costs while improving performance.
items.desc: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. items.desc: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. items.summary: The paper introduces Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), derived from a canonical dependence matrix, which provide optimal low-rank, reward‑independent representations for zero‑shot policy improvement in reinforcement learning.
items.why: It offers a theoretically grounded method to reuse knowledge across RL tasks, potentially boosting transfer efficiency and reducing the need for task‑specific reward engineering.
items.desc: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. items.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Model for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
items.summary: StereoVLM introduces the first geometry‑aware binocular vision‑language model that learns metric 3D spatial reasoning from calibrated stereo pairs via hierarchical training from disparity to depth and semantics.
items.why: It demonstrates that VLMs can be grounded in precise 3D geometry, enhancing the reliability of spatial reasoning for AI applications.
items.desc: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. items.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
items.summary: A 31‑billion‑parameter Gemma model solves 78 % of TEA‑Bench‑BR clinical coding tasks and passes over 99 % of hidden cases, while the 12‑B model solves far fewer.
items.why: It demonstrates that large coding agents can reliably implement complex, branching clinical specifications, a step toward safe AI‑driven healthcare software.
items.desc: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.

items.title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
items.summary: DistDNA characterizes LLMs by their prompt‑conditional response distributions and uses promptwise maximum mean discrepancy to identify models despite stochastic decoding variations.

items.desc: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. items.title: SLP‑Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
items.summary: The new SLP‑Bench benchmark shows that zero‑shot reasoning audio language models achieve only 52‑58% claim accuracy on clinical speech, but fine‑tuning a 7B model with GRPO raises accuracy to 60%.
items.why: It exposes the current limits of audio language models in clinical contexts and offers a concrete method to make their acoustic reasoning more reliable.
items.desc: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. items.title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
items.summary: The paper proposes three higher‑order attention mechanisms—conditional mutual information decomposition, contiguous token correlations, and a generalized maximum‑entropy formulation—to enrich the autoregressive probabilities used by decoder language models.
items.why: Improved attention can increase the information content of LLM predictions, potentially leading to better generation quality and more efficient decoding.
items.desc: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. A third introduces correlations between a set of key and query tokens and uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to obtain an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. All these methods may enhance the information content of the autoregressive probabilities that are used in inference/generation. Applications to contrastive decoding and a systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities are presented.

items.desc: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch

items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
items.summary: PlayCraft is an automated framework that uses a vision‑based agent’s play experience to iteratively revise games toward mastery‑level engagement.
items.why: It demonstrates how AI agents can autonomously improve game design, reducing the need for extensive human playtesting.
items.desc: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. items.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self‑Supervised Latent Action Learning
items.summary: The authors introduce O²LaF, which reuses a pretrained video diffusion transformer as a shared prior for both inverse and forward dynamics, achieving state‑of‑the‑art few‑shot action probing and zero‑shot transfer across navigation and manipulation tasks.
items.why: It demonstrates that generative video models can provide powerful priors for learning actionable representations without labeled data, boosting data efficiency in robotics and embodied AI.
items.desc: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings

items.title: AgentRoboCritic Analyzes Frontier Agents' Direct Robot Control Capabilities
items.summary: The paper introduces AgentRoboCritic, an intent‑grounded critique framework that evaluates action‑level performance of frontier multimodal agents, showing strong zero‑shot manipulation and recovery but exposing grasping and alignment bottlenecks.
items.why: It gives developers and researchers fine‑grained insight into the strengths and limits of next‑generation language agents for robot control.
items.desc: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. items.summary: LLM agents autonomously discovered, validated, and patched real‑world software vulnerabilities before 2026, with open‑weight models later matching this capability as disclosed vulnerabilities doubled in 2026.

items.desc: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. items.title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
items.summary: OracleImitator, a new active feature acquisition method that distills an explicit oracle teacher, matches or outperforms prior approaches while recovering up to 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at less than a quarter of the acquisition cost.
items.why: It offers a more cost‑effective way to select informative features, improving performance in budget‑constrained domains such as medical diagnosis.
items.desc: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. items.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.summary: PGX framework splits long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation into a predicate-based state machine, VLA skill phases, and world-coordinate locking to improve execution reliability.
items.why: It demonstrates how integrating classical control structures with vision-language-action models can overcome current limitations in complex robot tasks.
items.desc: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. items.summary: A hybrid BM25‑semantic retrieval system for Maharashtra government schemes achieves up to 0.879 MRR, modestly outperforming a strong lexical baseline.

The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. items.summary: AutoMaster automatically designs skill‑guided fine‑tuning interventions that improve teacher rollouts, boosting 4B and 9B model performance by 1.42–8.99 points over vanilla SFT.

items.summary: GLiDE introduces a family of 0.4B‑27B parameter decision models distilled from reasoning teachers that achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance (e.g., 71.52 hidden‑set score for the 27B model) with a single forward pass and calibrated confidence.

items.desc: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. items.summary: Rad‑Linter, which combines a pretrained image classifier with a 1.5 B‑parameter LLM fine‑tuned via LoRA, attains 98.5% pair accuracy—substantially higher than an 80.5% rule‑based baseline—on controlled chest X‑ray report and score pair evaluations.

items.desc: Rad-Linter checks chest X-ray reports against image-derived evidence to flag potential errors for review.
